title: Authentication vs. Authorization
oneLiner: Two different questions every request has to answer: who are you, and are you allowed to do this?
keyTakeaway: Authentication proves identity (401 when it fails); authorization decides what that identity may do (403 when it fails). Whatever does the authenticating, the app must only trust identity that arrived through it -- if a caller can skip the login and claim to be someone, nothing after that matters.
explanation:
The two words sound alike and get mixed up constantly, including in HTTP itself. Authentication ("authn") is proving who you are: a password, a Microsoft sign-in, a certificate, a code from your phone. Authorization ("authz") is deciding what a known person is allowed to do: everyone can read lessons, only Ava can erase Ava's progress. A failed authentication is a 401 (the status is named "Unauthorized", which is misleading -- it means "I don't know who you are"). A failed authorization is a 403 Forbidden: "I know exactly who you are, and no."

A common setup for an internal app, the one in the demo below, shows the split. The app never sees a password. It sits behind the company's ingress (the entry point that routes outside traffic into the Kubernetes cluster), whose login middleware does the Microsoft Entra ID sign-in and then forwards each request with a header naming the user (x-ms-client-principal-name). The app reads that header and decides what you can see: authentication outsourced, authorization kept. Most companies' internal apps work this way, so one team gets single sign-on right instead of every app writing its own login.

That design has one sharp edge, shown by the last caller in the demo. The app trusts the header blindly, so if anyone can reach the app without going through the ingress, they can send the header themselves and become anyone. The fix isn't in the app's code; it's making sure the ingress is the only way in, which is why such a setup includes a Kubernetes network policy that refuses connections from anywhere else.

Rules of thumb: check authorization on the server for every request (hiding a button in the UI is not access control); deny by default and allow specific cases; and give each person and service the least access that lets them do their job.
